intro: Kimiko Ishizaka plays the Fugue in B minor, BWV 869, the last fugue in Book I of The Well-Tempered Clavier. Its subject moves in semitones and uses all twelve notes of the chromatic scale, and the fugue is in four voices.

sections.label: A · Alto, tenor, bass, then soprano
sections.mNote: The four voices enter in turn with the chromatic subject

sections.label: B · Descending bass, alto entry returns
sections.mNote: Short imitations separate the complete subject entries.

sections.label: A′ · Tenor entry in E minor
sections.mNote: The subject enters in new keys, with closer imitation.

sections.label: A″ · Four voices close together
sections.mNote: Subject entries begin one bar apart.

sections.label: C · Running notes towards F♯ minor
sections.mNote: The semiquavers lead to the tenor’s next entry

sections.label: B′ · Tenor as bass line
sections.mNote: Soprano and alto exchange figures above the tenor

sections.label: Coda · Dominant pedal on low F♯
sections.mNote: The alto states the subject above the dominant pedal.

sections.label: D · B major under a fermata

cues.title: Fugue subject, alto
cues.text: After a short rest, the alto begins F♯–D–B. Wide leaps connect pairs of notes a semitone apart. Before this long subject ends it has touched all twelve notes of the chromatic scale, and it closes on F♯.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 1–4, alto; Mutopia edition, https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Subject in the bass
cues.text: The bass states the subject in B minor, F♯–D–B again, now in the lowest voice. Above it the tenor descends B–A–G♯–F♯ in crotchets, and the alto plays a quicker line of dotted notes and semiquavers.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 9–12: bass subject, tenor crotchets B–A–G♯–F♯ in bar 10, alto dotted-quaver and semiquaver figures. Mutopia edition (LilyPond source, notes.lyi), music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Soprano entry of the subject
cues.text: The subject reaches the highest voice after entries in alto, tenor and bass. Under the soprano’s F♯-minor answer, the bass plays a slower descending line in bars 13–16.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 1–16: entries in alto, tenor, bass and soprano; descending countersubject in the bass at bars 13–16. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Descending bass sequence, bars 17–20
cues.text: The bass descends in a sequence of short four-note patterns. Above it, soprano and tenor imitate each other in a quicker figure, with notes tied across the beat. In bar 19 the alto plays the first three notes of the subject and then drops out.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 17–20: descending bass sequence, soprano–tenor imitation and alto fragment in bar 19. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Subject in the alto
cues.text: After the episode the alto brings back the complete subject, F♯–D–B, in B minor. Above it the soprano descends B–A–G♯–F♯ in crotchets, the same countersubject the tenor played in bar 10.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 21–24: alto subject F♯–D–B–G–F♯–B–A♯, soprano crotchets B–A–G♯–F♯ in bar 22. Mutopia edition (LilyPond source, notes.lyi), music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Tenor entry in E minor
cues.text: The tenor enters with the subject in E minor, beginning B–G–E. The bass plays E and then rests. Above, the soprano descends in slower notes while the tenor moves through the semitone pairs of the subject.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 30–33: tenor subject, bass rest after E and soprano countersubject. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Marriage to Anna Magdalena Wilcke, 1721
cues.text: On 3 December 1721 Bach, then music director at the Köthen court, married Anna Magdalena Wilcke, a court singer there. In 1722, the year on the title page of Book I, he began looking for a new post.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv Leipzig chronology, 1717 and 1721 entries, for the appointments, marriage and 1722 job search: https://www.bach-leipzig.de/en/neutral/johann-sebastian-bach-%E2%94%80-chronology. Book I’s autograph title page is dated 1722.

cues.title: Stretto, four entries
cues.text: The soprano begins in B minor, and a bar later the alto enters in E minor. The bass follows in A major, then the tenor in D major. Each voice enters before the previous statement of the subject has finished, an overlapping of entries called stretto.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 41–47. Entry order and keys also tabulated at https://tonic-chord.com/bach-prelude-and-fugue-no-24-in-b-minor-bwv-869-analysis/.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Tenor entry in F♯ minor
cues.text: The tenor enters with C♯–A–F♯ and carries the subject into F♯ minor. Its continuation uses B♯ and F𝄪. Above it the soprano moves in longer notes.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 53–56: tenor entry in the second half of bar 53, B♯ and F𝄪 in bar 55. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Tenor entry in B minor, bar 60
cues.text: After the entries in F♯ minor and E major, the tenor begins F♯–D–B late in bar 60, back in B minor. Above it the soprano and alto continue with their tied notes and running figures.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 53–63: tenor entries in F♯ minor (bar 53) and bass entry in E major (bar 57), then tenor F♯–D–B late in bar 60. Mutopia edition (LilyPond source, notes.lyi), music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Episode without bass, bars 64–70
cues.text: Soprano and alto exchange the episode’s quick figures in imitation. The bass rests, and the tenor plays the lowest line, stepping down in sequence through the small patterns heard earlier. The bass re-enters in bar 70.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 64–70: soprano–alto imitation, tenor sequence, bass re-entry in bar 70. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Dominant pedal on F♯, bars 74–75
cues.text: In bars 74–75 the bass holds F♯, tied across the bar line, while the alto plays F♯–D–B, the opening of the subject, for the last time. The F♯ is a dominant pedal and postpones the arrival on B. Above it the soprano holds a suspended B, which resolves to A♯.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 74–75: bass F♯ tied across the bar line, alto subject fragment and soprano B–A♯ suspension. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Final chord in B major
cues.text: The four voices end on a chord of B major, B–D♯–F♯, in bar 76. The D♯ replaces the D♮ of the home key. This raised final third is known as a Picardy third, and the chord is held under fermatas in the outer voices.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bar 76: B–D♯–F♯, with fermatas in the outer voices. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: Bass sequence under tied notes
transitions.from: A · Alto, tenor, bass, then soprano
transitions.to: B · Descending bass, alto entry returns
transitions.how: After the soprano’s answer, the bass descends in repeated four-note groups. Above it, soprano and tenor alternate tied notes and semiquavers. The soprano’s E is held over a bass D and then resolves downwards. At the end of the sequence the bass moves from A♯ up to B, and the alto enters with the complete subject in B minor.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 17–21: bass sequence, soprano suspension across bars 19–20 and alto entry in bar 21. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.

transitions.title: D♯ leads the bass to E
transitions.from: B · Descending bass, alto entry returns
transitions.to: A′ · Tenor entry in E minor
transitions.how: The descending sequence in the bass ends on D♯, which rises to E, and the bass then stops. The tenor begins B–G–E, a complete statement of the subject in E minor, and the soprano plays the slower descending line that accompanies it. The tenor had already played three notes of the subject in bar 28.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 28–33: tenor fragment, bass D♯–E and tenor subject. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.

transitions.title: Running semiquavers lead towards F♯ minor
transitions.to: C · Running notes towards F♯ minor
transitions.how: In bars 50–53 the D-major entries lead into running semiquavers. The soprano climbs from D, and the alto follows with a similar figure from E. E♯ then appears in the alto and turns the harmony towards F♯ minor. The bass descends A–G♯–F♯ and stops. The tenor begins the next subject later in the same bar.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 50–53: upper-voice runs, alto E♯ and tenor entry after the bass withdraws. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.

transitions.title: Tenor takes the low line
transitions.from: C · Running notes towards F♯ minor
transitions.how: In bars 64–70 the bass voice is silent and the tenor plays the descending sequence. Above it, soprano and alto exchange the tied notes from the earlier episode. The tenor’s final A♯ rises to B, and the tenor then plays a shortened statement of the subject in B minor. The bass enters underneath in E minor, and the two low voices overlap.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 64–70: tenor sequence and shortened subject, then bass entry. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.

transitions.title: The last chord turns major
transitions.from: Coda · Dominant pedal on low F♯
transitions.to: D · B major under a fermata
transitions.how: The bass climbs chromatically to F♯ and holds it under the alto’s last subject fragment. The soprano’s B resolves to A♯ and rises to B as the bass moves F♯–B. In the alto, E falls to D♯. This raised third makes the final chord B major, held under a fermata.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1866), bars 73–76: chromatic bass ascent, dominant pedal, soprano suspension and final B-major chord. Mutopia edition, music ID 1563.

composer.epithet: Composer who supplied music for Leipzig’s churches for twenty-seven years and wrote a large body of keyboard music.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education. In 2006 some of his schoolboy copies of north German organ works, including two of the hardest pieces of the day, were found in the Anna Amalia Library in Weimar.

In 1702 he won the organist’s post at Sangerhausen, until the duke intervened and gave it to someone else. The next year Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and on 17 October married his second cousin Maria Barbara at Dornheim. The cantata for the inauguration of Mühlhausen’s town council in February 1708, Gott ist mein König, BWV 71, was one of the few works printed in his lifetime. In his cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, one voice sings the psalmist’s plea while another sings a hymn in long notes above it.
